title: Genie Code in action - An end-to-end demo.
transcriptText:
Genie code is an autonomous AI partner
for data teams.
We're going to see how it helps me
across data exploration, machine
learning, pipeline development, and
visualizing insights in a dashboard.
We start from an empty notebook with
Genie code open.
I can reach it by clicking this button
in the top right.
Let's start by asking for four insights
on the Wonder Bricks properties table.
You can see that by using the at symbol,
I can easily search across assets
including tables, notebooks, but also
dashboards and others
to make it easy for me to select them.
I'm going to also specify that I want to
see visualizations.
Genie code starts by reading the table
structure, understanding the metadata,
the columns available, and so on, and
also gathering some sample data to help
it with this exploration.
We see that it created an agent plan
towards the top right.
This allows it to track
where it's progressing in the task and
makes it easy for us to follow along as
well. This is really great for
long-running tasks where the agent is
working over several hours so that I can
see what it's doing.
It added the first insight to the
notebook where it's doing some setup on
the Wonder Bricks palette
and the first insight.
It now added the remaining three cells.
And before executing them, it gives me a
chance to review.
I can click always allow in the current
thread to speed things up a bit.
And we see the first insight has
executed.
Price distribution by property type,
new listings by property type,
and so on.
It has renamed the notebook to convey
what we've done here.
And at the end of its response, it
summarizes the insights in the chat with
links to the cells clearly marking all
the different insights that it has
gathered.
Now we're done with data exploration,
let's move to machine learning.
Now, before I switch
over to the notebook,
I want to show you how I built it. So,
this is a different tab where I prompted
Genie code to train an XGBoost model to
predict the price from the properties
table and join it with the destinations
table.
It loaded the data, did some exploratory
analysis,
did some hyperparameter tuning to find
the best model parameters, and then
trained the model and logged it to
MLflow.
So, switching back to our original tab,
I'm going to open that notebook over
here, the properties price prediction.
I'm going to say
in this notebook,
compare the model with random forest.
Skip hyperparameter
tuning just so that it goes a little bit
faster.
Right, so we ideally want it to pick up
from the XGBoost analysis that was
already done
and then do some comparison with a
different way to train the model.
We can see that Genie code added two
cells at the end of the notebook.
One for training and evaluating random
forest
and the final one for model comparison.
And it creates some nice visualizations
to compare them as well as a clear table
in the chat at the end
to tell us that XGBoost wins on all the
test metrics.
Awesome. So, from here I can ask Genie
code to go and deploy the model. I can
ask it to do further exploration
or even go to a deployed model and help
me configure it, optimizing it based on
the production traffic that we're
seeing.
But now I want to switch over to some
data engineering.
Now, switching tabs again, I want to
show a Spark declarative pipeline that I
built earlier, again with Genie code. I
prompted it to create a medallion
architecture pipeline with the samples
Wonder Bricks tables.
I've briefly defined what should be in
the bronze, silver, and gold layers and
asked it to run the pipeline. And we can
see that it created the tables, it
validated them, and ran them.
It also included this table properties
where for each layer it includes the
gold, bronze, or silver as the quality.
I want to take a a pause here and
explain instructions in Genie code.
Now, over here I'll open this
instructions file that I accessed
through the settings.
Instructions are a way for me to teach
Genie code about my preferences or
conventions.
So, here I have the Wonder Bricks brand
palette. This is what we saw earlier.
For all the visualizations, it set this
up and used the colors in the
visualizations.
For declarative pipelines, it's also
asked to include table properties with
the quality set to the medallion layer.
This is a great way to kind of establish
these conventions across all the work
that I do.
And but this is just the the personal
preferences. There's also workspace
instructions that an admin can set up to
ensure everyone in the workspace kind of
follows the same best practices.
But let's switch back to the pipeline
and I'll switch to the tab where we were
training the model.
I'll ask to navigate to
the Wonder Bricks
pipeline
editor page so we can continue working
on that pipeline and build it out a bit
further.
And now we're in the pipeline editor.
So, this is the right place for me to
build Spark declarative pipelines, but
I'm still within the same Genie code
thread. So, it maintains the context and
knows what we've done so far. So, I can
now ask it to add a gold feature table
for the price prediction model
and run it.
We can see that it added
the gold price prediction features file
and now it's updating it
with the Spark declarative pipelines
code to create it.
It's asking for permission before
running or dry running the pipeline to
validate things.
And now it's asking to run the pipeline
update just on the one data set
that we created here. Right, so it's
automatically being efficient even
though I didn't kind of have to specify
to just focus on that.
So, it looks like the gold feature table
is now live
and Genie code has summarized
the features and the sources that it
created in this table.
And from here I can add expectations, I
can preview the feature table data, and
so on.
But now I want to switch over to
building a dashboard with some of the
insights from the data that we've
created here.
So, I'm actually going to go and create
a new dashboard.
I'm going to close the filters tab just
to give us a bit more space.
And I'm going to ask Genie code to
create a dashboard
with five visualizations
from the gold tables in our pipeline.
We can see that it added
a nice header
and some charts visualizing
insights from our gold tables.
And now we see a summary of all the
insights.
And Genie code has completed its work.
So this is just a glimpse into what
Genie code can do across data bricks.
